questions.solution:
**Amoeba** splits into two equal daughter cells — binary fission.

Hydra and yeast reproduce by **budding**, Planaria by **regeneration** (a cut piece grows into a whole animal).

questions.q: Which of these is an example of vegetative propagation?
questions.solution:
A **cutting** grows into a plant genetically identical to its parent — vegetative propagation.

It is used for plants that make few viable seeds (banana, sugarcane, rose) and when the grower wants **exactly** the parent variety. Every commercial banana plant is effectively a clone.
options: A mango grown from a seed
A rose grown from a cutting
A bird hatching from an egg

questions.q: The male reproductive part of a flower is the:
questions.solution:
The **stamen**, made of a filament and an anther (which produces pollen).

The female part is the **pistil** — stigma, style and ovary.

questions.q: Fertilisation in humans normally takes place in the:
questions.solution:
In the **fallopian tube (oviduct)**.

The fertilised egg then travels down to the uterus and implants in its thickened lining, where the placenta develops to nourish the embryo.

questions.q: Which of these is a surgical method of contraception?
questions.solution:
**Vasectomy** in males (the vas deferens is tied) and tubectomy in females (the fallopian tubes are tied) are **surgical**.

Condoms are a barrier method, oral pills are hormonal, and the Copper-T is an intrauterine device. Only barrier methods also protect against sexually transmitted infections.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are present in a normal human body cell?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{46}$ — 23 pairs. The gametes carry half that number, $23$, so fertilisation restores $46$.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are present in a human sperm cell?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{23}$ — the haploid number.

Halving in the gametes is essential: otherwise the chromosome number would double every generation.

questions.q: How many parts does a pistil have (stigma, style, ovary)?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{3}$ — the **stigma** receives the pollen, the **style** is the tube it grows down, and the **ovary** holds the ovules.

questions.q: What is the approximate human gestation period, in months?
questions.solution: About $\mathbf{9}$ months, or $280$ days from the last menstrual period.

questions.q: What is the approximate length of the human menstrual cycle, in days?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{28}$ days, though anything from $21$ to $35$ is normal.

If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened uterine lining is shed — that is menstruation.

questions.q: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction, and explain why sexual reproduction is important for evolution.
questions.solution:
**Asexual reproduction**

• One parent; no gametes; no fertilisation.

• Offspring are **genetically identical** clones.

• Fast and needs no mate — an advantage in a stable, favourable environment.

• *Examples:* binary fission in Amoeba, budding in Hydra, spores in Rhizopus, vegetative propagation in plants.

**Sexual reproduction**

• Two parents; gametes fuse at fertilisation.

• Offspring show **variation** — they resemble both parents but are identical to neither.

• Slower and needs a mate.

**Why it matters for evolution.** Variation is the raw material natural selection works on.

A population of clones meets a new disease or a changed climate with **one** answer: if that answer is wrong, everything dies. A varied population is likely to contain a few individuals who happen to cope, and those survive and breed.

Variation arises in two ways: **crossing over** during meiosis, and the random combination of two parents' genes at fertilisation.

The banana is the cautionary example — commercially grown bananas are clones, and a single fungal disease has already destroyed one worldwide variety and is now threatening the next.

questions.q: Describe pollination and fertilisation in a flowering plant, and state the difference between self- and cross-pollination.
questions.solution:
**Pollination** — the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.

• **Self-pollination:** within the same flower or another flower of the same plant. It guarantees seed, but gives little variation.

• **Cross-pollination:** between flowers of **different plants** of the same species, carried by wind, water or insects. It gives variation, but depends on the carrier arriving.

**Fertilisation.**

1. The pollen grain lands on the stigma and germinates, growing a **pollen tube** down through the style — a chemotropic response.

2. The tube carries the male gametes to the ovule.

3. One male gamete fuses with the egg — **fertilisation** — forming the zygote.

**After fertilisation:**

• The zygote becomes the **embryo**

• The ovule becomes the **seed**

• The ovary becomes the **fruit**

• The petals, sepals, stamens and stigma usually wither and drop off

The fruit's purpose is dispersal — an animal eats it and carries the seeds away, so the seedling does not compete with its own parent for light.

questions.q: Describe the human male and female reproductive systems and the changes at puberty.
questions.solution:
**Male system.**

• **Testes** — make sperm and the hormone **testosterone**. They hang outside the body in the scrotum, because sperm production needs a temperature about $2$°C below body temperature.

• **Vas deferens** — carries sperm onward.

• **Prostate and seminal vesicles** — add fluid, giving the sperm nourishment and a medium to swim in.

• **Urethra** — the shared exit for urine and semen.

**Female system.**

• **Ovaries** — hold the eggs (all of them present from birth) and make oestrogen. One egg is released roughly each month.

• **Fallopian tubes** — carry the egg; **fertilisation happens here**.

• **Uterus** — where the embryo implants and develops. The **placenta** forms, giving the embryo glucose and oxygen and taking its wastes away.

• **Cervix and vagina**.

**Changes at puberty.**

*Common:* growth spurt, hair in the armpits and pubic region, oilier skin and often acne, new emotional intensity.

*Boys:* the voice deepens, facial hair appears, the chest broadens.

*Girls:* the breasts develop, menstruation begins, the hips broaden.

All of it is driven by hormones — testosterone and oestrogen — released on a signal from the pituitary gland. The wide variation in **when** puberty starts is entirely normal.

questions.q: What is contraception? Describe the four types of contraceptive methods and their advantages.
questions.solution:
**Contraception** — deliberately preventing pregnancy.

**1. Barrier methods** — condoms, diaphragms. They physically stop the sperm reaching the egg.

*Advantage:* they are the **only** methods that also prevent sexually transmitted infections, HIV included.

**2. Hormonal methods** — oral pills, implants. They change the hormonal balance so that no egg is released.

*Disadvantage:* side effects are possible, since the whole endocrine balance is being altered.

**3. Intrauterine devices** — the copper-T, placed in the uterus to prevent implantation.

*Advantage:* long-lasting and reversible. *Disadvantage:* can cause irritation or bleeding.

**4. Surgical methods** — vasectomy in men, tubectomy in women. The tubes carrying the gametes are blocked.

*Advantage:* permanent and highly reliable. *Disadvantage:* effectively irreversible, and needs surgery.

**Why it matters.** Contraception allows families to be planned, protects the mother's health by spacing births, and helps control the growth of a population against limited resources.

A separate and serious point: using these methods for **sex determination** — ending a pregnancy because of the child's sex — is illegal in India and has badly skewed the sex ratio in several states.

questions.q: Describe five methods of asexual reproduction with an example of each.
questions.solution:
**1. Binary fission** — the parent cell divides into two equal daughter cells. *Amoeba, Leishmania* (which divides along a fixed plane, because of its whip-like flagellum).

**2. Multiple fission** — the parent divides into many daughter cells at once. *Plasmodium*, the malarial parasite — which is why the fever comes in waves as the cells burst out together.

**3. Budding** — a small outgrowth forms, grows, and detaches. *Hydra, yeast.*

**4. Fragmentation** — the body breaks into pieces, each growing into a new individual. *Spirogyra.* This works only for simply organised creatures, where no piece is missing anything essential.

**5. Regeneration** — a cut piece regrows the whole organism, using specialised cells. *Planaria, Hydra.* Regeneration is **not** the same as reproduction: it is a repair mechanism that happens to be able to go that far.

**6. Spore formation** — thick-walled spores survive harsh conditions and germinate when things improve. *Rhizopus*, the bread mould.

**7. Vegetative propagation** — a new plant grows from a root, stem or leaf. *Potato (eyes), Bryophyllum (leaf notches), sugarcane, rose.*

The thread running through all of them: one parent, no gametes, and offspring that are genetic copies.
